record.paper_title: Problems and Conjectures Presented at the Third International Conference on Permutation Patterns (University of Florida, March 7-11, 2005)
record.original_question: Consider a general t-stack sorting machine, where one asks whether a given input permutation can be sorted using t stacks in series under some sequence of legal moves. Can this decision problem be solved in polynomial time, or is it NP-complete?

evidence.quote: By allowing any sorting algorithm we reach the definition of general t-stack sortability.
Problem (Mike Atkinson): Can one decide in polynomial time whether an input permutation is sortable by a general t-stack sorting machine, or is this problem NP-complete?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider t stacks arranged in series, where t ≥ 2 is a fixed integer. The sorting machine receives an input permutation π of {1, 2, …, n} on its left, has access to t stacks S_1, S_2, …, S_t arranged left to right, and produces an output sequence on its right. At each step, exactly one of the following "legal moves" may be performed:
(i) pop the next element of the input and push it onto S_1;
(ii) for some 1 ≤ i ≤ t − 1, pop the top of S_i and push it onto S_{i+1};
(iii) pop the top of S_t and append it to the output.
The permutation π is said to be sortable by the general t-stack sorting machine if there exists some sequence of legal moves (chosen with full knowledge of π, not restricted to any greedy or deterministic policy) that processes every element of π and produces the identity 1, 2, …, n as output.

Decision problem: Given a permutation π of {1, 2, …, n} as input, decide whether π is sortable by the general t-stack sorting machine.

Determine the computational complexity of this decision problem. Specifically, is there an algorithm that solves it in time polynomial in n, or is the problem NP-complete?
artifact.status_search_result: The case t = 2 was resolved by Pierrot and Rossin (2014, published 2018), who showed that deciding sortability with two stacks in series can be done in polynomial time. For general t ≥ 3, the complexity of recognizing general t-stack sortable permutations remains open according to recent surveys on stack-sorting disciplines.

status_evidence.title: 2-Stack Sorting is Polynomial
status_evidence.snippet: A polynomial algorithm is given to decide whether a given permutation is sortable with two stacks in series.
status_evidence.claim: The t = 2 case is in P.

status_evidence.title: 2-Stack Sorting is polynomial (STACS 2014)
status_evidence.snippet: Decision problem of 2-stack sortability proved to lie in P, a longstanding open problem since Knuth.

status_evidence.title: A survey of stack-sorting disciplines (Bóna)
status_evidence.snippet: Nothing is known about the enumeration of sortable permutations for t-stacks except when t = 1; complexity of deciding sortability remains a longstanding open problem.
status_evidence.claim: For general t the decision problem's complexity remains open.
